content:
Most of the advice about UK PhD funding assumes you win a studentship. But there is a quieter, non-competitive route that gets far less airtime: the Postgraduate Doctoral Loan from Student Finance England. For courses starting in the 2026/27 academic year, you can borrow up to £31,122, paid to you over the length of the doctorate, to spend on fees or living costs as you choose. There is no merit test, no interview and no supervisor selection hurdle — the filter is residence, age and academic history.

Who qualifies

The scheme is for students ordinarily resident in England who are UK nationals or hold settled status, with three years of ordinary UK residence before the course starts. You must be under 60 on the first day of the first academic year, and the course must be a full standalone doctoral programme of three to eight years — not a top-up, not a professional doctorate wrapped around employment in some cases, and not a second doctorate. Two exclusions do the most damage in practice: you cannot take the loan if you already hold a doctorate or equivalent, and you cannot hold it alongside Research Council funding — a UKRI studentship and the doctoral loan are either-or, which is why the choice between them deserves its own thinking (our comparison of UKRI stipend rates covers what the funded alternative pays).

How the money arrives

You apply once for the whole course — not yearly — and Student Finance England confirms the yearly amount as each year begins. The total is split evenly across the course and paid in three instalments per academic year, straight into your bank account after your university confirms attendance to the Student Loan Company. Your National Insurance number must be on file before anything moves, and the money is yours to allocate: many part-time and self-funded PhD students put it entirely toward fees, while full-time students on cheap programmes use most of it as a living allowance. Note what the loan does not include: doctoral students cannot claim the Childcare Grant, Adult Dependants' Grant or Parents' Learning Allowance that master's students on the taught-loan scheme can access.

Repayment: how it actually works

Repayment follows the postgraduate loan rules: you repay a percentage of income above the postgraduate threshold, and the doctoral balance is combined with any master's loan you took — the two debts repay together, while your undergraduate loan runs concurrently rather than merging. Interest accrues from the day of the first payment, and anything unpaid is written off after the standard term. The honest framing for a PhD borrower is this: the loan turns a doctorate into a long-term income-linked obligation rather than an upfront cost, which for applicants targeting academia-adjacent or public-sector careers is often the only viable bridge — and far cheaper in practice than its headline size suggests for those whose incomes stay moderate.

Deadlines and the devolved-nation difference

There is one rule to diary: apply within nine months of the first day of the last academic year of your course. Missing it forfeits the loan retroactively, so even late-deciders who started a PhD self-funded can often still apply — the window closes only nine months before your final year ends. You can now apply online for 2026/27 starters, and the passport details form matters more than people think because identity evidence delays are the most common hold-up. Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland run different doctoral support — Welsh students face a separate funding model rather than this loan — so "England" is doing real work in the scheme's name. If you are an international applicant, this scheme is not open to you; your routes are the competitive ones in our UK PhD funding guide and the scholarship schemes in our Chevening and Commonwealth guides.

Loan or studentship: a decision framework

If you have a funded studentship offer, take it — the studentship is free money and the loan is not available alongside it. The loan's real audience is the applicant with an offer but no funding, the part-time doctoral candidate whose employer will not pay, and the researcher who wants the freedom to design their own project outside a DLA's portfolio. Run three numbers before deciding: your course's annual fees, your city's living costs, and the gap the loan leaves — £31,122 over three years is roughly £8,650 a year, which alone will not fund most full-time PhDs and needs savings, family support or part-time work behind it.

The choice also has a career dimension. Studentships come with supervisor structures, cohort peer groups and a funding office that keeps you on schedule; the loan route buys independence at the price of isolation, and completion rates for unfunded doctoral students are consistently lower. Neither path is wrong — but decide with the arithmetic in front of you rather than the label "fully funded" doing your thinking for you.

University awards to apply for alongside the loan

The loan rarely covers a whole PhD, so pair it with university money — even a partial fee waiver stretches it dramatically. Each competition below is live; two consider you automatically with your course application.

  • Leeds Doctoral Scholarship 2027 — Leeds' central doctoral competition. Deadline: 23 March 2027, 17:00 UK time.
  • University of Edinburgh Doctoral College Scholarships - Fully Funded PhD — Edinburgh's Doctoral College scholarships
  • Interdisciplinary Chancellors Scholarships at University of Warwick 2027 — Warwick's interdisciplinary Chancellors scholarships. Deadline: 10 December 2026, 16:59 GMT (course: 7 December; references: 21 December).
  • College Research Awards in the Business School at University of Edinburgh 2027 — Edinburgh Business School research awards. Deadline: 2 February 2027, 23:59.
  • Wolfson Postgraduate Scholarships in the Humanities at the University of Nottingham — Wolfson scholarships in the humanities at Nottingham. Deadline: 19 January 2027, midday.
  • Bristol PGR Scholarships in Health and Life Sciences at University of Bristol 2027 — Bristol’s health and life sciences PGR awards
